title: Still arguing, for heaven's sake
hookLine: Jews still argue over law, for heaven's sake
carry: an argument for heaven's sake endures
last: LIVE BY THEM, NOT DIE BY THEM.

cards: Two schools of sages, the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, disagreed about marriage law. Not about table manners: about which marriages were valid at all, which is about as high as the stakes get.
Each side, by its own reasoning, could look at some of the other's marriages and see a problem. And the Mishnah reports what happened next. They married into each other's families anyway.
They kept arguing, and the families kept joining. Today's word is how a tradition manages that.

teach.h: FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN, IT ENDURES.
teach.b: Still arguing. You met the Mishnah's test last year; today, what it asks of an argument. First, the test.
Pirkei Avot says that every argument for the sake of heaven will in the end endure, and every argument not for the sake of heaven will not endure.
In Hebrew, machloket l'shem shamayim: an argument about what is true and right, not about winning. Second, the examples. Which argument was for the sake of heaven?
The argument of Hillel and Shammai. Which was not? The argument of Korah and all his company, the rebellion against Moses in the wilderness.
Some readers notice an odd detail: for Hillel and Shammai, both sides are named. For Korah, Moses isn't named as a side at all.
One reading: Korah's company was never really arguing with Moses. Each of them was arguing for himself. Third, the wedding.
That's what makes the report about marriage so striking.
The two houses disagreed where it mattered most, and still did not stop marrying into each other's families. The argument and the relationship both survived. Fourth, today.
Jews are still arguing over law. Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist Jews read the tradition differently, and inside each, rabbis disagree again, as the last two days showed.
In a study hall, a learning partner is supposed to push back; a quiet room might mean nobody's thinking.
The Mishnah's question still sits on every argument: is this for heaven's sake, or for mine?

how: Jewish learning is often done aloud with a study partner, a chavruta, whose job is to question and push back. Rabbis and movements publish differing rulings and debate them openly.

o: a debate held only by rabbis in a court
arguing for heaven's sake, and staying together
a quarrel that never gets settled at all

p: not for the sake of heaven
in the end, it does not endure

s: the Mishnah says every argument will last
only an argument for the sake of heaven; one that isn't will not endure.
Hillel's and Shammai's houses married into each other's families
the Mishnah reports it, even though they disagreed about marriage law itself.
the Mishnah's bad example is 'Korah and Moses'

games.q: you're in the house of Shammai. you disagree with Hillel's house on marriage law itself, and the stakes are real. a family from Hillel's house proposes a match. what do you do?
o: refuse, and stop speaking to them.
keep arguing, and marry into each other's families anyway.
agree only if they switch to your view.
games.why: the Mishnah reports the houses did not refrain from marrying each other. the argument and the relationship both survived.

practice: Bring to mind one disagreement you're in right now, and picture the other person at a table you both belong to: a meal, a meeting, a wedding. Ask gently whether you're arguing for what's true or good, or to win.
Then ask what would keep you both at this table, whatever the answer.

wordCard.voice: Still arguing. Machloket l'shem shamayim: an argument for the sake of heaven, the kind the Mishnah says will endure. Today's word.
